section_summary: This closing section contains public protests and a petition urging the United States to stop exports of arms, lead, oil, scrap iron, and other war materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies explain that the Neutrality Act could embargo arms only after a presidential proclamation of war—which would affect China as well as Japan—and did not authorize restrictions on commodities such as lead. The section also includes guidance on American property-damage claims against Japan and a cross-reference to a Chinese study of Japan’s ability to finance war-material purchases.

subfiles.title: Concluding page of Mrs. W. D. Boone’s protest concerning Japan
subfiles.about: The fragment argues that delayed American action emboldens Japan to continue destruction and killing.
subfiles.summary: Closing page of Mrs. W. D. Boone's letter, mostly illegible, condemning deliberate delay and urging stronger action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. W. D. Boone
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the legal limits on restricting exports to Japan and provides procedures for American claims arising from Japanese military action in China.
subfiles.summary: State tells Mrs. Boone a war finding would bar arms to China and Japan and no authority exists otherwise; licenses since July 1, 1937 were $14,218,523.21 for China and $10,793,865.38 for Japan; it explains how nationals and missionary groups may file claims for Japanese-caused losses.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on language for replying about claims against Japan
subfiles.from: B. M. English, Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: The memorandum supplies proposed language concerning Japanese responsibility for American property losses and the filing of claims.
subfiles.summary: Legal Adviser's office recommends telling the writer the U.S. notified Japan it will seek compensation where international law makes it liable, and directing claimants to file via the nearest American office in China or with the Department.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to booklet on Japan’s ability to finance war-material purchases
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects researchers to file 894.51/599 for a Chinese Council for Economic Research booklet on Japan’s war-purchasing finances.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to file 894.51/599: a Chinese Council for Economic Research booklet on Japan's ability to finance war-material purchases.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding a petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.about: The sender forwards a petition concerning the Japanese invasion of China for the President’s serious consideration.
subfiles.summary: Degraded letter to Roosevelt enclosing a petition on the Japanese invasion of China; State's reply identifies it as Mr. Haskell's October 8 letter.

subfiles.title: Petition to the President on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.from: W. W. Haskell and other petitioners, principally from the West Plains, Missouri, area
subfiles.about: The petition asks the President to use every practical means to end American trade that supports Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Petition accuses Japan of violating the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact, condemns bombing of civilians, says American aircraft, scrap and oil sustain aggression, and requests action to end the traffic; two pages of signatures follow.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. W. Haskell regarding the petition
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the petition and explains why the President had not invoked the Neutrality Act against arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: State tells W. W. Haskell a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to China and Japan, invocation was judged against U.S. interests, non-arms goods aren't covered; licenses were $14,265,554.11 for China and $10,793,865.38 for Japan.

subfiles.title: Alfred C. Schmitt’s protest against sales of war materials to Japan
subfiles.about: Schmitt protests the sale of American war materials and lead to Japan for use against the Chinese people.
subfiles.summary: Alfred Schmitt, citing a photo of a Japanese ship loading American lead for bullets, contrasts missionary work with permitted exports and calls the traffic wicked and inhuman.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Alfred C. Schmitt
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that existing neutrality legislation did not authorize the President or Secretary of State to prohibit exports of lead to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State tells Schmitt a Neutrality Act proclamation would bar arms to both countries, the act covers only enumerated arms and lead isn't included, so no authority exists; licenses were $14,265,554.11 for China and $10,793,865.38 for Japan.
